summary: The Incident Object Description Exchange Format defines a data representation for security incident reports and indicators commonly exchanged by operational security teams. This proposed standard describes an updated information model for IODEF and a data model specified in XML.

plainLanguage.summary: The Incident Object Description Exchange Format (IODEF) version 2 defines a shared way to exchange security reports and signs of malicious activity. It uses Extensible Markup Language (XML) and includes requested responses and rules for handling shared information.

subtitle: A structured XML format for sharing security incident reports, response requests and threat indicators.

tldr.problem: Security teams need to exchange incident reports, threat indicators, and response information with other organizations. The format needs enough structure for automated processing while allowing flexible information.
tldr.mechanism: IODEF defines an information model and an XML schema for incident details, events, indicators, requested actions, and sharing instructions. It also provides defined ways to add data and enumerated values.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7970 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 5070 and RFC 6685. It adds indicator support to the earlier incident-report format, with some incompatibilities with version 1.

today: RFC 7970 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2016. It obsoletes RFC 5070 and RFC 6685; the unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Teams Share Incident Information
sections.content:
Organizations sometimes need help from other parties to respond to malicious activity. They may ask an Internet service provider to filter attack traffic, contact another site about a botnet, or share watch lists of known indicators.

The Incident Object Description Exchange Format (IODEF) represents information commonly exchanged by Computer Security Incident Response Teams (CSIRTs) and other operational security teams. It carries indicators, incident reports, response activity, and metadata in an XML format that supports machine-to-machine exchange and automated processing.

The RFC describes IODEF as a transport format, not necessarily the best format for archiving or in-memory processing. It also notes that sharing has procedural, cultural, legal, and trust barriers that the format does not address.
sections.plainLanguage: IODEF gives incident response teams a shared format for exchanging reports and signs of malicious activity. It supports automated handling, but it does not solve legal, trust, or coordination barriers.

sections.title: Data Types and Translated Text
sections.content:
IODEF assigns data types to information so that systems can interpret it consistently. Integers and real numbers MUST use base 10; binary data can use base64 or hexadecimal; and an enumerated type is an ordered list of accepted keywords. A date-time represents one instant, not a range.

The ML_STRING type holds text that people read. Its optional xml:lang attribute identifies the language, while translation-id can link translated versions under the same parent. The generic EXTENSION type carries information the standard does not otherwise represent, with attributes that identify its data type and meaning.
sections.plainLanguage: The format labels each item as text, a number, a date, or another defined kind of value. It can mark the language of text and group translated versions.

sections.title: The Document and Incident Model
sections.content:
An IODEF-Document contains one or more Incident classes and may contain additional extension data. Its required version value is 2.00. Each incident has an IncidentID, a GenerationTime, and at least one Contact; its purpose states why it is being shared, and its optional status records its workflow state.

Other incident fields can record when activity was detected or occurred, how it was discovered, its assessment, methods used, event details, indicators, and a handling history. RelatedActivity can connect an incident to other activity and describe a threat actor or campaign.

The restriction attribute gives disclosure guidance for a class and its children. A child can set a different restriction. The RFC says this is only a guideline: IODEF has no technical way to make a recipient follow it.
sections.plainLanguage: An IODEF document contains one or more incident reports. Each report identifies the incident, its creation time, and at least one contact; sharing labels guide recipients but cannot enforce their choices.

sections.title: Events, Impact, and Requested Actions
sections.content:
EventData describes individual events within an incident, while Incident holds the overall summary. Event details can include times, contacts, discovery information, systems, records, assessments, and requested actions. EventData can nest to group related details, and when a detailed event conflicts with the incident summary, the more specific event data MUST take precedence.

An Assessment can describe technical, business, time, monetary, or intended impact, with a confidence estimate. An Expectation records what the sender asks the recipient to do, such as investigate, block traffic, or watch for an indicator. It can name a desired start time and an end time; if the recipient cannot complete the action before that end time, the recipient MUST NOT carry it out.
sections.plainLanguage: An incident can contain smaller event descriptions that add detail. A report can describe the effects and request actions, but the recipient must not carry out an action it cannot finish by the stated deadline.

sections.title: Indicators and Observable Features
sections.content:
Version 2 adds indicators: observable features or patterns that can help detect malicious activity. Each indicator has an identifier and may include a description, a period of validity, confidence, contacts, and references. Its defining content MUST be exactly one of an Observable, an IndicatorExpression, an ObservableReference, or an IndicatorReference.

An Observable describes one feature, such as an address, domain, email, file, certificate, or a bulk list of values of one type. An IndicatorExpression combines observables or other indicators with Boolean operators: not, and, or, or xor. Nested expressions act like parentheses, and invalid algebraic expressions MUST NOT be specified.

The observable-id attribute lets an indicator refer to an observable already described elsewhere in the document. Indicator start and end times can limit when the indicator is considered valid.
sections.plainLanguage: An indicator describes something that can be observed to detect malicious activity. It can name one observable feature or combine several with rules such as AND or OR.

sections.title: XML Processing and Language Support
sections.content:
Every IODEF document MUST begin with an XML declaration that states the XML version and character encoding. UTF-8 SHOULD be used unless UTF-16 is necessary, and other encodings SHOULD NOT be used. The document uses the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:iodef-2.0 and MUST reference the IODEF schema with xsi:schemaLocation.

Documents MUST be well-formed XML. The RFC RECOMMENDS schema validation, but schema validity alone does not ensure semantic validity because some constraints are explained only in the text. Implementations SHOULD update their schemas periodically as registered enumerated values change.

Each document MUST identify its language, normally on the top-level element. Free-form text may specify a different language, and matching translation-id values link translations. Implementations SHOULD select text in a language relevant to the recipient.
sections.plainLanguage: A report must be valid XML and name its IODEF version, encoding, and language. Checking the XML schema alone may miss rules written in the specification's text.

sections.title: Extensions and IANA Registries
sections.content:
IODEF can grow through new enumerated values and extension classes, but adding attributes to existing classes is not supported. A private enumerated value uses the value ext-value in the original attribute and puts the new value in its corresponding ext- attribute. A public value can be added to the applicable IANA registry.

The EXTENSION type can carry atomic values or XML. XML extensions MUST use a separate namespace. Implementations MUST NOT download schemas at runtime unless appropriate precautions are taken, and recipients MUST be prepared for a referenced schema that cannot be resolved.

The RFC creates 34 IANA registries for enumerated values, with Expert Review as the allocation policy. It also registers the IODEF namespace and XML schema.
sections.plainLanguage: Teams can add new values or extra data when the standard has no matching entry. IANA can list shared new values, but the format does not support adding new attributes to existing classes.

sections.title: Changes from IODEF Version 1
sections.content:
RFC 7970 evolves the incident-report data model in RFC 5070. The changes are largely additive and include indicators, observable identifiers, classes for threat actors and campaigns, and additional data for describing incidents.

Some changes are incompatible with version 1. The document version changes to 2.00; multilingual strings use xml:lang; Service@ip_protocol becomes Service@ip-protocol; and several classes or fields were removed, renamed, or made optional. For example, ReportTime is no longer required, while GenerationTime is required.
sections.plainLanguage: IODEF version 2 adds indicators and new incident details to the earlier format. Some fields changed, so version 1 documents may need edits before they can be used as version 2 documents.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
The information in an IODEF document may be sensitive. The protocol used to exchange documents MUST provide confidentiality, integrity, and authenticity. Implementations also need to authenticate senders and recipients because they may act on requested actions or other document data.

Recipients may reassess confidence values, and MUST ignore a confidence element when it is unclear which data it describes. Some values, including confidence ratings and defined courses of action, require agreement outside the document before operational exchange. Implementations MUST handle executable or machine-readable content carefully to prevent unintended execution.

Identifiers can be linked to people or organizations, and repeated exchanges can enable correlation. The RFC says to share personal identifiers only when necessary and to protect documents with transport-level confidentiality. The restriction attribute remains guidance that a recipient may ignore.
sections.plainLanguage: IODEF reports may contain sensitive details and content that software can act on. The exchange must protect the report from disclosure and changes, confirm who is communicating, and handle executable content carefully.
